description: Hip flexor stretch for desk workers, drivers and runners: how to do it, how it supports the pelvis, common mistakes, easier and harder versions.
intro: The hip flexor stretch targets the muscles at the front of your hip, which get short and stiff with long sitting and can pull on the pelvis. It does not train the pelvic floor. It helps the hips and pelvis move freely, so the pelvic floor can work and relax more easily.
feel: You should feel a stretch at the front of the hip and upper thigh on the back-knee side, with the back glute lightly squeezed and your torso tall. If you feel it mostly in your lower back, you are arching. Self-check: if the stretch disappears when you stop arching, keep the glute squeeze and shift forward less.

mistakes.wrong: Arching your lower back to go further
mistakes.right: Tuck your tailbone slightly and keep your ribs over your hips. A small shift with a level pelvis is enough.
Move only an inch or two. Once you feel the front of the hip, stop and breathe.

mistakes.wrong: Clenching the pelvic floor along with the glute
mistakes.right: Squeeze the glute, but keep your belly and pelvic floor relaxed.

easier: Pad the back knee, hold a chair for balance, or do it standing with one foot back. Shorter 15–20 second holds are fine.
harder: Raise the arm on the back-knee side overhead and lean slightly away from it. Hold the full 30 seconds each side with slow breathing.
who: Good for desk workers, drivers, runners and cyclists, and anyone who feels stiff in the hips or lower back after sitting.
skip: Modify it if kneeling hurts your knees, or if you have groin pain, a hernia or recent hip or abdominal surgery. In pregnancy, hold onto something and keep the range small. Stop if it hurts.

faq.q: Do tight hip flexors affect the pelvic floor?
faq.a: They can affect how your pelvis sits and how much tension you hold around it. Stretching them is not a pelvic floor treatment, but it can make sitting and standing more comfortable.

faq.q: Can I do this stretch at my desk?
faq.a: Yes. Stand, step one foot back, squeeze that glute and shift forward slightly while holding the desk. It makes a good break after long sitting.
